title: Broadband Purcell Filter for Fast Superconducting Qubit Reset and Readout
authors: Yu Zhao, Zhixu Chen, Hanxian Liu, Mingze Liu, Zixing Liu, Hao Pang, Meiyan Wan, Changkun Wu, Liuzhu Zhong, Sai Li, Yuefeng Yuan, Yuxuan Zhou, Ji Jiang, Ji Chu, Song Liu
abstract: Rapid reset and readout of qubit states are essential for quantum error correction, yet accelerating these operations through stronger coupling to a dissipative environment inevitably increases qubit decay via the Purcell effect. Here we present a broadband Purcell filter that decouples the reset and readout paths, enabling both operations to be independently optimized without compromising qubit coherence. The filter employs two engineered notches - an intrinsic notch and a bandstop notch - to provide broadband Purcell protection, together with an additional reset stub that creates a reset mode below the protected band. To enable fast reset while suppressing filter-mediated interactions between qubits, we couple each qubit to a dedicated reset resonator. We experimentally demonstrate Purcell-limited relaxation times exceeding 1 ms across a 1.2 GHz bandwidth, simultaneously with 500 ns readout without a Josephson parametric amplifier and 100 ns reset with 99.6% efficiency. The reset resonator is designed with a deliberate kappa-chi mismatch, which suppresses photon-shot-noise-induced dephasing by a factor of 70 compared to the readout resonator. Our work provides a scalable hardware solution that resolves the traditional trade-off between fast qubit operations and qubit protection, advancing the prospects for fault-tolerant quantum computing.
summary: This paper presents a novel broadband Purcell filter for superconducting qubits that resolves the conflict between fast quantum operations and qubit coherence. By engineering the filter with distinct notches and a dedicated reset stub, the authors achieve coherence times over 1 ms while maintaining fast readout and reset capabilities. This provides a critical hardware advancement for scalable quantum computation.
main_problem: Accelerating qubit reset and readout operations for Quantum Error Correction (QEC) typically increases qubit decay via the Purcell effect, creating a fundamental trade-off.
main_result: The authors designed a broadband Purcell filter that decouples reset and readout paths, achieving Purcell-limited coherence times exceeding 1 ms over 1.2 GHz while enabling fast (100 ns) reset and 500 ns readout.
method: The work involves designing and experimentally implementing a superconducting microwave filter structure incorporating intrinsic and bandstop notches, alongside dedicated reset resonators.
model_or_system: The system uses superconducting qubits coupled to a microwave filter on a flip-chip processor. The architecture utilizes engineered notches and a dedicated reset stub to create a low-frequency reset mode, allowing independent optimization of the readout and reset channels.
key_observables: Purcell-limited relaxation time ($T_{1,P}$), readout time (500 ns), reset time (100 ns), and dephasing suppression factor (70).
important_parameters: 1 ms coherence time over 1.2 GHz bandwidth; 99.6% reset efficiency; $\kappa-\chi$ mismatch for dephasing suppression.
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is that decoupling the reset and readout paths via engineered filter components can resolve the inherent trade-off between speed and coherence.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the physical layout and circuit schematic of the filter, the measured transmission spectrum showing the protected bands, and characterization plots comparing measured $T_1$ to the theoretical Purcell-limited lifetime.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by identifying the Purcell decay problem, proposing a broadband filter architecture with decoupled reset/readout paths, detailing the experimental implementation and characterization of the filter's spectral properties, and finally presenting measurements demonstrating fast, high-fidelity operations alongside long coherence times.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses hardware limitations in superconducting quantum computing by providing a scalable, engineered solution to the Purcell decay problem, which is crucial for building fault-tolerant quantum processors.
